::: {#explain .lx-sec}

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="t5-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Capacity factor</dt><dd>Energy made ÷ (size × hours): the share of the most a plant could make that it actually made.</dd>
<dt>Same MW, different MWh</dt><dd>In 2025, U.S. nuclear plants ran at 91.1% of their size on average, wind at 33.8% and solar at 24.0%.</dd>
<dt>Every hour counts</dt><dd>Nights and calm hours stay in the count, which is why solar's capacity factor is low.</dd>
<dt>The cube law</dt><dd>Below the rated speed, twice the wind speed gives eight times the power.</dd>
<dt>Rated and cut-out speeds</dt><dd>Above the rated speed the output stays flat; in a storm the turbine stops.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Capacity factor depends on the period and the place</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The same fleet has a different capacity factor every month. In 2025, U.S. wind ran at 23.1% in September and 43.1% in March; solar at 13.1% in December and 31.9% in June and July; nuclear at 81.0% in October and 99.2% in December, with the dips in the spring and fall refuelling seasons (EIA, Table 6.07.B).

- **Availability is not capacity factor.** A solar farm can be ready all night and still make nothing.
- **Curtailment lowers it.** A wind farm turned down by the grid makes less than its weather allowed ([lesson 0](00-grid-operator.qmd)).
- **Sites differ.** The U.S. averages hide windy plains and sunny deserts; Prairie Town's shapes come from one region.

Lesson 7 uses capacity factor to spread a plant's building cost over the MWh it makes.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The power curve, from physics to measurements</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The power carried by wind through a rotor of swept area $A$ is $P_\text{wind} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$. For the lesson's turbine (a 100 m rotor, air at $\rho = 1.225$ kg/m³) at its rated speed of 12 m/s that is 8,313 kW, and the turbine makes 3,000 kW: a power coefficient $C_p = 0.36$. No turbine can beat the Betz limit, $C_p \le 16/27 \approx 0.593$.

The clean [power curve]{.lx-term term="power-curve"} in the lesson is

$$
P(v) = \begin{cases}
3000 \times (v/12)^3 \text{ kW} & 3 \le v < 12 \text{ m/s}\\
3000 \text{ kW} & 12 \le v \le 25 \text{ m/s}\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$

A measured power curve is a cloud of 10-minute records around such a line: gusts, air density, the wakes of other turbines and the turbine's own controls move each point. Estimating a farm's curve, with its uncertainty, from scarce records is a research problem in its own right; one approach combines a theoretical curve with measurements in a multi-fidelity Gaussian process ([Li et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1115/DETC2023-114762); open framework: [mfgpr-wind-power-curve](https://github.com/Henryutd2021/mfgpr-wind-power-curve)). Modeler lesson M9 (upcoming) fits one, and bridge B2 (upcoming) computes capacity factors from a year of hourly data in Python.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The wind and solar shapes are whole regional fleets, smoother than any single farm.</li>
<li>Wind and solar use the shared “power” scaling, output = size × shape<sup>g</sup>: each month matches the U.S. average and the best hours reach full size. The seasons are national; the hours are those of one region.</li>
<li>The nuclear plant's outage and the turbine are illustrative, not a real plant or model.</li>
<li>Air density changes with temperature and altitude, which shifts a real power curve.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="t5-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="full" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A 100 MW wind farm makes 100 MW most of the time.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In 2025, U.S. wind farms made 33.8% of what they would have made at full size, and the cube law makes their output swing with every change in the wind.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="broken" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A solar farm with a 24.0% capacity factor is broken three-quarters of the time.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At night and under clouds it works as designed: the sun, not the machine, sets most of the gap.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="double" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Doubling the wind speed doubles a turbine's output.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Below the rated speed it multiplies the output by eight (2 × 2 × 2); above the rated speed the output stays flat.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="t5">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 50 MW solar farm made 105,120 MWh in a year of 8,760 hours. What was its <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span>?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">24.0%</li><li data-value="b">48.0%</li><li data-value="c">12.0%</li><li data-value="d">100%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>24.0%: 105,120 ÷ (50 × 8,760) = 0.240. Using only daytime hours would double it; using 100 MW would halve it.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mwh" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">At the 2025 U.S. average of 91.1%, how much <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> does 1 MW of nuclear make in a year?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">8,760 MWh</li><li data-value="b">7,980 MWh</li><li data-value="c">911 MWh</li><li data-value="d">91.1 MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>7,980 MWh: 1 MW × 8,760 h × 0.911. The full 8,760 MWh would need every hour at full size.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
